name: Back sleeping pillow setup

card.summary: Using pillows to stay on your back at night, which looksmaxxers hope will even out one-sided facial changes; no study tests that outcome.
card.note: Sleep position effects on facial shape have not been studied in the sources reviewed; back sleeping is associated with positional sleep apnea in some people.

quick.overview:
A back sleeping pillow setup uses pillows placed beside the body or under the neck and knees to discourage rolling onto the side or face during sleep. Looksmaxxing users adopt it because they believe sleeping on one side contributes to facial asymmetry, wrinkles or flattening.

No published study identified here has tested whether sleep position changes facial shape. Sleep research does document health associations of different positions.
quick.mechanism: Pillows act as physical barriers or supports so the sleeper stays supine. The community theory is that continuous pressure on one side of the face during sleep affects soft tissue or skeletal development over time.
quick.risks: Sleep literature associates back sleeping with positional obstructive sleep apnea in a large share of OSA cases and with more frequent sleep paralysis. Positional therapy that discourages back sleeping is used for apnea.

lead: A back sleeping pillow setup is an arrangement of pillows meant to keep a sleeper lying on the back instead of on one side or the stomach. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to avoid pressure on one side of the face overnight.

Users on looksmax.org have described attributing their worse-looking side to the side they sleep on, with one poster reporting acne and asymmetry concentrated on the side they favour and asking how long it takes to get used to back sleeping [1]. Other replies in that thread attributed asymmetry to genetics [1].

General sleep literature describes lateral sleeping as the most common adult position, followed by back and then stomach sleeping [2]. No study identified for this article tests pillow arrangements for changing facial appearance.
infobox: Stay supine to avoid facial pressure

paras: Setups commonly described by users use bolster or body pillows on either side of the torso, and sometimes support under the knees, to make rolling over less likely. Individual designs vary and no single configuration is standard.

Lateral sleeping tends to increase with age and body mass index, and one proposed explanation is that back sleeping produces more awakenings [2]. Positional obstructive sleep apnea accounts for roughly 56 to 75 percent of regular OSA cases, and positional therapy that discourages back sleeping is used to reduce it [2]. Back sleeping is also linked to more frequent sleep paralysis, and right-side sleeping to more nighttime reflux than left-side sleeping [2].
One user in the looksmax.org thread linked his side sleeping to acid reflux, which fits the general finding that left-side sleeping is considered the better position for reflux symptoms [1][2].

No studies found on pillow setups or sleep position as a cause of facial asymmetry. A 2002 trial in a manipulative-therapy journal examined a bedding system and sleep quality, back pain, shoulder pain and spine stiffness, which is outside facial appearance [3].

lore.intro: Posters on looksmax.org discuss sleep position as a possible source of asymmetry and ask about switching to back sleeping [1].

claims.claim: Sleeping on one side causes the "bad" side of the face to look worse
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster reports that all of his unfavourable asymmetry and extra acne is on the side he sleeps on, and asks about adapting to back sleeping [1].
claims.experts: No published study identified here has examined whether sleep position affects facial shape; other forum replies attribute asymmetry to genetics [1].
